reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: A group of glomerular diseases defined by dominant C3 deposition on immunofluorescence with little or no immunoglobulin, reflecting dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway
It encompasses dense deposit disease (DDD) and C3 glomerulonephritis, distinguished mainly by the appearance of deposits on electron microscopy
Patients may present with haematuria, proteinuria (sometimes nephrotic range), hypertension, and variable degrees of kidney impairment
Serum C3 is often low while C4 is typically normal, consistent with selective alternative pathway activation
Underlying drivers include acquired autoantibodies such as C3 nephritic factor and genetic or acquired defects in complement regulatory proteins (e.g. factor H, factor I, CFHR abnormalities)
Dense deposit disease can be associated with acquired partial lipodystrophy and retinal drusen
Evaluation includes a complement functional and genetic workup and screening for monoclonal gammopathy in older adults, which can drive complement dysregulation
The disease frequently recurs after kidney transplantation, and complement-targeted therapies are an area of active development
reference.pathophysiology: C3 glomerulopathy results from uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway. Normally this pathway is tightly regulated by proteins such as factor H and factor I; when regulation fails, through acquired autoantibodies (notably C3 nephritic factor, which stabilises the alternative pathway convertase) or genetic and monoclonal-driven defects, excessive C3 is cleaved and its breakdown products deposit within the glomerulus. This leads to a proliferative glomerular injury with dominant C3 staining and scant immunoglobulin. In dense deposit disease the deposits form characteristic dense osmiophilic transformation of the basement membrane, whereas C3 glomerulonephritis shows more discrete mesangial and capillary wall deposits.
additionalDifferentials: Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (as a related complement disorder)
additionalInvestigations: Serum complement profile (C3, C4) and alternative pathway functional assays
Testing for C3 nephritic factor and autoantibodies to complement regulators
Genetic screening of complement genes (e.g. CFH, CFI, CFHR)
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and free light chains, especially in older patients
Kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy for definitive diagnosis
redFlags: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with declining kidney function
Features of an underlying monoclonal gammopathy in older adults
reference.prognosis: The course is variable but a substantial proportion of patients progress to kidney failure over years, and disease commonly recurs in transplanted kidneys; outcomes depend on the underlying complement abnormality and response to treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for resolving post-infectious glomerulonephritis and missing persistent complement dysregulation
Failing to pursue a complete complement and genetic workup
Overlooking an underlying monoclonal gammopathy driving disease in older patients
